content: Sylvite is the natural mineral form of potassium chloride (KCl). It crystallizes in the isometric system, exhibiting a structure that closely resembles that of halite (sodium chloride, NaCl). In fact, sylvite and halite are isomorphous, meaning they share the same crystal structure. The mineral is typically colorless to white, but it can display shades of yellow or red due to the presence of inclusions. Sylvite has a Mohs hardness of 2.5, indicating it is relatively soft, and a specific gravity of 1.99.490. Sylvite has a distinctly salty taste, accompanied by a characteristic bitterness. It is one of the last minerals to precipitate during the evaporation of saline solutions, which is why it is predominantly found in extremely arid, saline environments. The primary application of sylvite is as a potassium-based fertilizer, making it an essential resource in agriculture. This mineral is present in numerous evaporite deposits around the world. In the United States, significant bedded deposits of sylvite are located in New Mexico, western Texas, and Utah. However, the largest known deposits globally are found in Saskatchewan, Canada. These extensive deposits in Saskatchewan were formed through the evaporation of a Devonian seaway. Sylvite holds special significance in this region, as it is recognized as the official mineral of Saskatchewan. Sylvite was first identified in 1832 at Mount Vesuvius near Naples, Italy. It was named in honor of François Sylvius de le Boe (1614–1672), a Dutch chemist who made significant contributions to the field of science.
